articles.title: Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth
articles.content: Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on x (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on facebook (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on linkedin (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on x (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on facebook (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on linkedin (opens in a new window) Fitzcarraldo – inside the chicest publisher on earth on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Helen Bain . Photography by Wendy Huynh Published September 25 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. At the age of 29, Jacques Testard set up a publishing house because no one in publishing would employ him. Born in France and schooled in London, he had wanted to go into academia before a series of internships made him realise that publishing was “another way to be serious about books”. In 2014, when he struggled to find a permanent opening, he decided to launch his own house. His ambition was not just to be an editor but to find and publish “writers at the cutting edge of contemporary literature” – including, significantly, work in translation. He had 18 months until the money ran out. “I thought, ‘I’ll give this a go and see what happens, and maybe in a few years’ time someone will give me a job.’” Every publisher is a story, says Ray O’Meara, the house’s art director, and the story of Fitzcarraldo Editions is very simple. Twelve years ago, mainstream UK publishers did not believe there was a market for translated literature. It was a gap Testard was able to plug. The first book he published that year was Zone by Mathias Énard, a 521-page stream-of-consciousness account of an amphetamine-fuelled journey across Italy, written in a single sentence, which he had discovered when he read it in French. For the new house, it was something of a mission statement. That same year, still the sole employee, Testard made an offer for Svetlana Alexievich’s oral history Second-hand Time . The book was already a bestseller in Russia and had sold well in France and Germany but there was no competition for the UK rights. Testard’s opening bid of $2,000 was rejected; he upped it a little and it was accepted. The following year Alexievich won the Nobel Prize in Literature and there was an eight-way auction for the US rights. The publisher aims to select works that are “innovative, imaginative, ambitious” © Wendy Huynh Today, Fitzcarraldo Editions has become a hallmark for a generation. Its signature International Klein Blue and clean cream titles include Nobel- and Pulitzer-prize winners, with authors ranging from French memoirist Annie Ernaux to New York-based war reporter Jon Lee Anderson and Hong Kong novelist Dorothy Tse. It specialises in contemporary literary fiction and long-form essays, seeking out work that is determinedly “innovative, imaginative, ambitious”, broadly kept at a 50-50 split between English language and literature in translation. Cult hits include Perfection by Vincenzo Latronico , an interrogation of millennial life; The Plague , essays on death and humanity by PEN Pinter-award-winner Jacqueline Rose; and this year’s Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life: Voices From Gaza by Samar Yazbek. A poetry list launched last year: this May, American poet Sasha Debevec-McKenney won the Dylan Thomas Prize for her debut collection Joy Is My Middle Name , while Makenna Goodman’s novel Helen of Nowhere is currently longlisted for the Booker Prize. It’s an extraordinary outcome for a house that started out with a single employee, 18 months’ funding, and the modest aim of publishing six books a year. “I feel fortunate to have started a press when I did,” says Testard with understatement when we meet in Fitzcarraldo’s offices in a former factory in Peckham Rye, south-east London. “I guess I turned up at the right time.” Fitzcarraldo founder and publisher Jacques Testard © Wendy Huynh “Fitzcarraldo is forging ahead on its own path and terms,” says Harriet Moore, literary agent at Alexander Aitken. “They have a robust commitment to the long view, a confidence in their own sensibility and vision, and their books will last. It offers a place where writers can think seriously and strangely, work against the expected, follow their obsessions, play.” “Jacques is concerned about quality, not quantity,” says Norwegian writer Jon Fosse , who won the Nobel Prize in 2023; Fitzcarraldo had published Septology , a seven-part novel in a single sentence, the previous year. “He has trusted me.” Fosse had won numerous international awards, but his prose was not published in the UK until Fitzcarraldo released Scenes from a Childhood in 2018. “Jacques is an attentive editor who gives excellent advice and is deeply respectful of authors,” says Ernaux. The Years had been published to acclaim in France in 2008 but it was not until 2018 that Fitzcarraldo published the translation to a rapturous reception, credited as contributing towards Ernaux’s 2022 Nobel win. (Testard had argued the case to nominate it for the International Booker despite it being hybrid-memoir rather than fiction; it was shortlisted.) It now seems absurd that Ernaux, Fosse and Alexievich (as well as Nobel-winner Olga Tokarczuk , whose Drive Your Plow Over the Bones of the Dead is a Fitzcarraldo bestseller) had not been published in the UK sooner. Testard shrugs when this is put to him, pointing out that when Fitzcarraldo launched there was still a tendency in bookshops to shelve international literature in its own category, “almost labelling it as a separate genre”. He attributes this partly to a British Empire legacy; that with the Commonwealth there’s “a sense that you’re [already] bringing writers in from the peripheries”. There is also the commercial aspect – “this notion that translation is more expensive, and you’ll never be able to recoup the money”. But there is also the question of discovering it in the first place. Testard grew up reading “indiscriminately” in English and French, and he also reads Spanish. “There are very, very few editors in UK publishing who read in other languages,” he says. “In Spain or France or Germany you have to have three or four languages to be in the editorial positions we are in.” At the Fitzcarraldo Editions office in Peckham, south London. From left: operations executive Samir Chadha, associate publisher Tamara Sampey-Jawad, operations director Jennifer Tighe, editor Charlotte Jackson and editor and publicist Emma Berrill © Wendy Huynh Testard, 41, possesses the extreme courtesy often typical of his generation, underscored by a certain steel. Wearing a collarless blue shirt and dark trousers, he talks fluently and rapidly about how his frustrations with the anglophone publishing industry brought him where he is today. The open-plan space, now housing 11 employees, is all white walls and deep-blue accents, light pouring in from the Crittall-style windows. On an exposed brick wall at one end of the room, trademark blue-and-white spines are lined up in rows, while in the small, bare meeting room, coloured Post-Its stuck on a wall denote the year’s publishing schedule: non-fiction, fiction, poetry, classics. Outside, over the railway line, sits Peckham Levels, the multistorey car park turned cultural hub where Fitzcarraldo holds its annual party each summer. Testard’s gravitas echoes across the house – although sometimes this effect seems almost accidental. “Can we do that?”, O’Meara recalls wondering when Testard first suggested taking the name Fitzcarraldo from Werner Herzog’s 1982 film about an opera-loving fanatic rampaging around the Peruvian jungle. Your browser does not support playing this file but you can still download the MP3 file to play locally. Labour officials in Downing Street and beyond have discussed the parameters in which a snap election could be called. Will Andy Burnham take the gamble? As speculation about the idea grips Westminster, host Lucy Fisher is joined by political editor George Parker and deputy political editor Jim Pickard to weigh up the risks and rewards of going to the public early. They also look ahead to the Labour Party conference in Liverpool starting this weekend, and the troubles that lie ahead for UK-EU relations. Plus George reports back from Burnham’s first major international summit at the UN general assembly in New York, where the prime minister weathered his first encounter with Donald Trump. Follow Lucy on X or Bluesky @LOS_Fisher , @lucyfisher.ft.com ; George on @georgewparker.bsky.social , @GeorgeWParker ; Jim @PickardJE Want more? articles.title: In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait
articles.content: In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on x (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on facebook (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on linkedin (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on whatsapp (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on x (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on facebook (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on linkedin (opens in a new window) In Rome, a palazzo becomes a self-portrait on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Maria Shollenbarger . Photography by Ramona Balaban Published September 26 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. “I never really designed this space,” says 30-year-old artist and designer Paolo del Gallo di Roccagiovine. “It simply grew around my work.” We’re in an early-18th-century palazzo midway down the ruler-straight stretch of Rome’s Via del Babuino , three floors above the street’s neat ranks of artisan and designer boutiques. The grand, high-ceilinged apartment that del Gallo has welcomed me into has been owned by his family for generations; today its warren of rooms has been conscripted for his various artistic projects. A bed designed by del Gallo using a baroque headboard from the family collection © Ramona Balaban “Its last permutation was as my grandfather’s law office,” del Gallo continues. “At some point he emptied it completely, intending to figure out what to do with it at a later date.” Then Covid came. “My brother, my two sisters and I moved in very quickly to distance ourselves from our parents and grandparents.” Mattresses were thrown onto floors; in place of several of the doors, which had been sent out for restoration, del Gallo hung textiles he’d brought back from India and Uzbekistan. His siblings, he recalls, “arrived with large suitcases full of clothes. I apparently decided that my essentials for surviving lockdown were an antique gilt grotto table, a pair of beautiful chairs and some silver cutlery.” The 18th-century desk that he uses as his work table, covered in studies, drawings and raw materials © Ramona Balaban By 2022, he realised the apartment “had quietly filled itself with my things: paintings, materials, objects I’d collected”. So he came to an arrangement with his family to use it as his atelier – a place to work, receive clients and spend the occasional night in town. Del Gallo’s creative output moves between sculpture, painting, installation and interior-design intervention. Historical objects – a chair, a mirror, a book, a fragment of an ancient Ionic column capital – are “active structures” within his work. An antique hourglass is embellished with a hyperrealist rendering of an exotic butterfly; a pair of 18th-century doors are gilded in patterns like shards of light. An artwork from Paolo del Gallo’s 2025 show Butterfly Effect, along with ceramic sculptures, including one of his ancestor Zénaïde Bonaparte © Ramona Balaban His commissions range from tiny installation-like sculptures of shells and corals to entire ballrooms frescoed to residents’ specifications. Del Gallo’s work can be found across Rome: there’s a large mural inside Villa Europa, the official headquarters of the EU delegation, restoration work at the Belgian Embassy to the Quirinal and the former Belgian Embassy to the Holy See (the Belgian ambassador, Pierre-Emmanuel De Bauw, also owns his work) and pieces in private homes. At his mother’s mid-18th-century villa , the walls are covered in his dreamily atmospheric murals. Del Gallo with one of his artworks in the archive room © Ramona Balaban “What drew me to Paolo’s work was his sensitivity to nature and texture, coupled with his deep love for and integration of his own history,” says New York-based collector Tracey Hejailan-Amon. “What’s striking is how seamlessly these two registers coexist in his practice, and how easily they integrate with other artists’ works.” “Architecture is never simply a backdrop,” says del Gallo, tall and rangy, dressed in an old white button-down shirt with sleeves rolled up and loose trousers. He’s drawn to “spaces that already carry a strong sense of memory. When I work on historical surfaces, like mercury or mirror, it creates a trace that I couldn’t invent myself. I think of it as a kind of collaboration with time.” From left: a neoclassical marble oil lamp – one of his favourite pieces – painted doors he created for a 2021 exhibition at Palazzo Colonna, an oil on raw linen painting of an emu he painted while in Mexico and a door from Palazzo Sacchetti © Ramona Balaban An oil painting on an antique mirror – a work in progress © Ramona Balaban Time and history play an outsized part in del Gallo’s art. His family tree includes Napoleon Bonaparte and the Spanish royal family; he has lived most of his life in grand historic residences. His brothers and sisters pursued more conventional careers while he studied at Rome’s Accademia di Belle Arti. “I don’t remember ever deciding to be an artist,” he says. “I just grew up surrounded by art, and architecture.” At 16, he began practising restoration, which informed his later style; the natural-history books of his ancestor, ornithologist Charles-Lucien Bonaparte, “taught me very early to look closely at nature – its beauty, fragility and complexity”. He brought it permanently into his visual language. The main salon at  del Gallo’s family apartment in Rome has the original palazzo flooring and frescoes on the ceiling. He painted the mural on the walls using natural pigments such as lapis lazuli and Armenian earth © Ramona Balaban In the apartment’s main salon, “the principal theme is day and night”. A combination of stripping back layers of older paint and layering on new ones has resulted in vast semi-abstract murals of cloud and sky. On one wall, a cool white sun projects slightly from the surface; opposite, a pale moon is discernible through darker tones. Del Gallo’s delicate colours – rendered with rare materials such as lapis lazuli dust and Armenian soil – reprise the tones of the original ceiling frescoes. Two canvases, one hung midway up the wall and another leaning next to the fireplace (both unframed, as is del Gallo’s preference), echo the celestial theme at a more contained scale. The 18th-century chest of drawers in the bedroom is a Neapolitan piece. On top is a gilt crucifix from the private chapel of his family’s palace, a carved-bone pyramid and a vase he found in Mexico. He restored and painted the historic walls himself © Ramona Balaban Del Gallo’s penchant for the palimpsest has even reshaped the structure of his surroundings. “Sometimes I wake up convinced that there must be something hidden above a false ceiling, and decide to open it up. One day I imagined there was a fireplace behind a wall; I started drilling, and actually found it there, blocked up, with traces of soot inside.” Del Gallo crafted a new surround, mixing cement, lime and marble dust to create an unadorned frame that’s an elegant counterpoint to the ornate room. “I don’t only work in any one room,” says del Gallo. “It’s difficult to call a single space ‘my studio’ because in reality I make use of the whole apartment. It has become part of the creative process. Inevitably, it influences everything I do.” A corner room full of easels and tables “has the best light, and is where I store most of my materials”. A small but perfectly formed dining room, its walls hung with family porcelain, has a Carlo Scarpa table, covered in the same linen he uses for painting, at which he sometimes alights. The whole space is a locus for artistic experimentation that’s also as intimate and revealing a self-portrait as a home can be. articles.title: A warning of ‘breakdowns and deficiencies’ in security at the US central bank
articles.content: The Fed’s Office of Inspector General warned of potential security breaches at the US central bank © Reuters Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on x (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on x (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on facebook (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on linkedin (opens in a new window) Watchdog warns about Fed’s ‘deficiencies’ on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Abigail Hauslohner in Washington Published September 29 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected] Hello from Washington and welcome to White House Watch. Here’s what we’re looking at today: Federal Reserve’s watchdog warns of security “deficiencies” at central bank Marco Rubio blames a “foreign actor” for the UK terror plot over the weekend US completes withdrawal of troops from Iraq The Federal Reserve’s watchdog has warned of “breakdowns and deficiencies” in security at the US central bank after a departing official was suspected of removing sensitive information, highlighting vulnerabilities at the institution. The Fed’s Office of Inspector General flagged potential breaches by an unnamed employee in the international finance division, culminating in 279 “data loss prevention” alerts in the 90 days before they retired in July 2024, 111 of these potentially involved information relating to the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee and 40 potentially contained central bank material. “This potential incident highlighted information security risks and control breakdowns and deficiencies that we believe require the board’s immediate attention,” the watchdog wrote in a report released on Monday. Government officials have long harboured concerns about the security of the Fed, which is seen as a high-value target for foreign adversaries because of the board’s proprietary financial information. The watchdog recommended tighter security procedures, which the Fed agreed to implement, but it said there was insufficient basis to pursue a misconduct investigation into the matter. What’s next for the global economy? Economics leader writer Tej Parikh and European economics commentator Martin Sandbu will be answering questions on the next stage of growth, its biggest risks and how global businesses and households will be affected. Submit your question here for the latest instalment of Ask an Expert happening on Thursday October 1. The latest headlines US secretary of state Marco Rubio said a “foreign actor” was involved in a suspected terrorist plot near a British air force base this weekend, in remarks that will intensify global scrutiny of the incident . The US Treasury on Monday took its first concrete steps towards cracking down on a suite of strategies used by wealthy US investors to cut their tax bills . Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece has caused a political stir in Romania after suggesting the US could bring down governments. Trump asked Xi Jinping if China wanted to buy American weapons , US envoy says. Private equity has become an important target on the campaign trail for the US midterms as candidates blame large investors for soaring housing costs . Divisions within Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again movement risk damaging Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. What we’re hearing Happening under the radar this week: the US is completing the withdrawal of most of its forces from Iraq. You would be forgiven for thinking: ‘Didn’t this already happen?’ Yes, it did, in 2011. US forces returned to fight the Islamic State a few years later. And now, 23 years after the initial US invasion of Iraq, nearly all US troops are expected to withdraw from the country by tomorrow. Kurdish leaders in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region of Iraq’s north are unhappy. Masrour Barzani tells my colleague Mehul Srivastava that the Americans are leaving their Kurdish allies without any missile defences and vulnerable to Iranian attack amid a war started by Donald Trump six months ago. “The threat is real,” Barzani said in a recent interview. The abandonment by Washington is “shameful”. Could you be the FT’s next stock picking champion? The FT’s new Stock Picking Game is a fast, fun way to test your trading instincts, sharpen your market expertise and compete for the chance to win £1,000. Terms and conditions apply. Register for season two now. Viewpoints Democrats are likely to make gains in Congress in November’s midterm elections but a divided government is unlikely to derail Trump’s agenda , argues Edward Luce. Jonathan Derbyshire says that, although Republicans are outspending the Democrats by around $1bn to $750mn, they are heading for a historic defeat. For once, the Fed has put Main Street before Wall Street, writes Sheila Bair US accounting editor Stephen Foley highlights how requirements under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act are being rolled back. Your browser does not support playing this file but you can still download the MP3 file to play locally. Recorded in front of an audience at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, host Lucy Fisher and political editor George Parker unpack Andy Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. From rethinking Britain’s relationship with the EU to ending the pensions triple lock and scrapping the electoral system, Burnham laid out an ambitious agenda for the country. Lucy and George speak to business secretary Jonathan Reynolds about the prime minister’s plans, before northern correspondent Jennifer Williams and Inside Politics writer and columnist Stephen Bush join them to give their takeaways from the week. Want more? Free links: Andy Burnham sets up battle lines on social care and Europe How would Andy Burnham’s social care shake-up work? Get 30 days free. Political Fix was presented by Lucy Fisher and produced by Persis Love. Manuela Saragosa is the executive producer. Video editing, original music and mix by Breen Turner. While inflation in most nations has come down from its peak, many policymakers have warned that the last leg of the journey to central banks’ target — which in most advanced economies is 2 per cent — will be the hardest. Higher borrowing costs helped ease the fast pace of price growth that swept the world during the pandemic, but many countries have now entered a fresh cycle of lowering rates. But that changed, as this global animation shows. Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings. Post-pandemic supply chain disruptions and rising energy prices resulting from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine triggered a wave of inflation that left few countries untouched. articles.title: An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich
articles.content: An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on x (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on facebook (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on linkedin (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on whatsapp (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on x (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on facebook (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on linkedin (opens in a new window) An economist’s – and poet’s – guide to Zürich on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Jessica Salter . Photography by Joël Hunn Published September 30 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. I moved to Zürich from Geneva when I was four, but I was born in Munich. (My mother is Dutch and my father is German.) I moved back to Germany in my early teens, but I returned here to study economics at the University of St Gallen before completing another degree in economics and philosophy at Harvard. Now I split my time between London and Zürich, working in finance and investments along with writing and performing poetry. I feel very Swiss. Our first home was an apartment near Lake Zürich. But the home I really remember was further out in Schindellegi, a village that feels quite rural despite only being half an hour from the city centre. My childhood memories are mainly sensory: the mountains, the lake. Sound behaves very differently here than in most cities. You feel cocooned. The lake is central to life in Zürich ; when it’s warm, everyone gathers on the water’s edge at weekends and after work. I like sitting on the terrace at Alex Lake Zürich, a hotel right on the water (there’s a little boat that runs back and forth to Storchen, a hotel and restaurant in the city centre). On the northern shore, La Muña has a small rooftop terrace that’s perfect at sunset, with the whole city laid out below. A view of the Limmat river towards Lake Zürich © Joël Hunn Marktgasse in the city centre © Joël Hunn Having a treat there © Joël Hunn Everyone here is sporty and nearly everyone is a semi-professional cyclist. I’m not – I ride a Dutch bike with upright handlebars – and I prefer hiking to cycling. Üetliberg, a mountain just above the city, is the easiest hike; you can walk for a couple of hours. Etzel on the south side of Lake Zürich is a proper half-day walk and there’s a restaurant at the top. For a serious hike, I go to Grosser Mythen , a mountain with steep, hairpin turns. I have been going to Seebad Utoquai, the public baths on the promenade between Bellevue and Zürichhorn, since childhood. You can bathe in the lake too: people even swim to work with all their things in a waterproof bag. I’ve recently joined a group of female entrepreneurs who meet further down the lake towards Richterswil . We do a cold plunge in the lake, then help each other with business plans, funding and networking. On Römergrasse in the city centre © Joël Hunn At Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books © Joël Hunn L’Alsace Heureuse by Hansi on display there © Joël Hunn People think Zürich is very straight-laced, and on the surface it is. But behind closed doors, it’s radically creative. There’s a thriving techno scene: Adriatique and Jenny Cara are based here. In my early 20s, I had a DJ friend who would take me to Kreis 5, which is a bit like London’s Shoreditch. Basel and Zürich are notorious for hating each other because of football, but people come here from Basel for the music; they respect each other’s techno scenes. One of the most beautiful buildings here is the Schweizerische Nationalbank, right in the centre on Börsenstrasse. There is a building next door, the SNB Forum, where you can see bank notes and explore the history of SNB on an interactive LED screen. It also hosts the Karl Brunner Distinguished Lecture Series; I’ve heard American economist John H Cochrane speak there. Growing up in Zürich has been influential in teaching me how a European capital of finance conducts itself. There’s a big focus on family-owned businesses here, so naturally they think about how to exist for many generations. In New York or London, where I’ve also lived and worked, the pace is more rapid, which can feel quite short-term. At the shop of Swiss label Lamarel © Joël Hunn I’ve always spent more money on books than clothes. Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books in the heart of the old town is my favourite bookshop. It specialises in beautiful and rare books from the 15th to 21st centuries – I once found an early edition of one of Else Lasker-Schüler’s poetry collections – and the shop is a centre for literary minds and creatives. Zürich also has brilliant vintage furniture shops, such as Kioskio , which sources pieces from private collections across Europe; the prices are genuinely good. For clothes, I like Lamarel, a Swiss label built around simple, easy shapes. The city has different dress codes depending where you are: around the art schools and design studios in Kreis 4 and Kreis 5, the style is loose and vintage. In the centre it is more conservative, with muted tones and immaculate tailoring. Outside at Trattoria Neumarkt © Joël Hunn Eating a number of dishes there © Joël Hunn Green olives, stracciatella di burrata with chilli crunch and chive, and sourdough bread with miso butter © Joël Hunn The food scene has changed a great deal since I was a child. There used to be only a handful of restaurants serving international cuisine; now there are many. Amia is a new outdoor bar with a French Mediterranean-inspired menu, and I love the confit of char at Bürgli. Trattoria Neumarkt does rotating pop-up menus, often with a Japanese-Italian blend; I go for its Japanese take on cacio e pepe with udon noodles. My Italian partner was initially sceptical but has since been won over. When I want to write, I go to B2 Boutique Hotel, a former brewery near the Google offices that now has the most extraordinary library bar: books floor to ceiling, all the way round. I’ll sit there for hours with a coffee and write. But mostly I find myself going back to the lake. I go down to Bürkliplatz, a town square where you can sit right on the water. I find it endlessly inspiring. Zürich has taught me a sensitivity for atmosphere, silence and order. There’s a layer to the city that makes you attentive to what is not said, and that’s where poetry can happen. BARS, CAF´ÉS & RESTAURANTS Amia restaurantamia.ch Bürgli restaurantbuergli.ch La Muña lareserve-zurich.com Storchen Zürich storchen.ch Trattoria Neumarkt neumarkt-zuerich.ch SHOPPING Dr Peter Bichsel Fine Books finebooks.ch Kioskio kioskio.ch Lamarel shoplamarel.com THINGS TO DO Schweizerische Nationalbank snb.ch Seebad Utoquai Utoquai 50, 8008 WHERE TO STAY Alex Lake Zürich alexlakezurich.com B2 Boutique Hotel b2hotel.ch Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Follow the topics in this article Travel Switzerland Zurich How To Spend It In... articles.title: Ennis (EBF) Grows Sales but Earns Less. Are Legal Items Hiding a Better Business?
articles.content: Ennis (EBF) Grows Sales but Earns Less. Are Legal Items Hiding a Better Business? Jeff Lewis September 22, 2026 3 min read EBF Ennis, Inc. (NYSE: EBF ) reported higher sales and lower earnings for the quarter ended August 31, 2026, but legal items complicate the comparison. The underlying business held up better than the headline profit decline suggests, while paper costs created genuine margin pressure. The September 21 release showed revenue of $102 million, up 3.3% from $98.7 million. Net earnings fell to $9.4 million from $13.2 million. Investors need to distinguish the litigation effects from changes in demand, acquisition contributions, and production costs. Bull Case The prior-year quarter included a $5.3 million favorable litigation judgment, while the current quarter included an unrelated $700,000 litigation charge. Management said diluted earnings per share increased $0.02 after excluding these items from both periods. This non-GAAP comparison removes the specified litigation effects from reported diluted earnings per share. That modest improvement is more encouraging than the reported earnings decline. Gross profit also increased to $30.5 million from $30.1 million, showing that the larger revenue base produced additional gross profit despite a lower margin. Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) generated $34.1 million of operating cash flow in the first half, compared with $18.4 million a year earlier. Cash reached $54 million as of August 31, and management reported no debt. That financial position provides room to support operations and acquisitions without immediate refinancing pressure. Supply continuity is another positive. Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) has received shipments from alternative carbonless-paper suppliers following the closure of the sole domestic producer. Management continues to expect uninterrupted product availability and customer service. Maintaining supply protects the ability to fulfill orders while the business adapts to higher input costs. Bear Case Acquisitions contributed approximately $2.3 million of the $3.3 million quarterly revenue increase. Subtracting the disclosed acquisition contribution leaves roughly $1 million of additional sales, or about 1% of prior-year revenue, based on rounded figures. The reported growth rate therefore overstates the improvement outside those acquisition contributions. Gross margin declined to 29.9% from 30.5%, a decrease of 60 basis points. Management attributed the decline primarily to higher carbonless-paper costs recognized in cost of sales. That pressure affects the economics of producing and selling printed products independently of the litigation comparison. Story Continues Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) needs pricing, product mix, or productivity improvements to offset those costs. Reliable access to paper addresses availability, while purchasing terms and selling prices determine how much profit remains on each order. Cash generation also requires context. Inventory declined during the quarter after the earlier buildup to protect supply. Investors should assess whether operating cash flow remains strong once inventory levels stabilize, since working-capital movements can change cash generation without equivalent changes in earnings. Hedge Fund Sentiment The filings available so far reflect positions held before Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) reported its quarterly results. Insider Monkey's database showed 15 hedge funds holding Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) at the end of 2Q2026, up from 14 funds three months earlier. Conclusion Ennis, Inc. (NYSE:EBF) looks more resilient after accounting for the litigation items, supported by strong first-half cash generation and a debt-free balance sheet. However, acquisition contributions explain most of the quarterly sales increase, and paper costs are squeezing margins. Growth outside acquisitions, gross-margin stabilization, and cash flow after inventory normalization will determine whether the business is improving sustainably. articles.title: Strive CEO: Bitcoin Could ‘Go to Infinity' as Dollar Debt Crisis Breaks
articles.content: Strive CEO: Bitcoin Could ‘Go to Infinity' as Dollar Debt Crisis Breaks Darryn Pollock September 22, 2026 2 min read BTC-USD ASST DX-Y.NYB Strive CEO Matt Cole says Bitcoin (BTC) could effectively go to infinity against the US dollar, arguing that a mounting Washington debt crisis, not Bitcoin's own scarcity, is what will ultimately break the currency's value. Cole made the comments on Bloomberg Crypto, as digital assets have reclaimed $3 trillion in market value since January. Strive, a Bitcoin treasury company that raises capital to buy and hold BTC on its balance sheet, has been one of the more aggressive buyers through the cycle. A Debt Crisis, Not a Bitcoin Story Cole argued that the 10-year Treasury yield would already sit north of 10% if the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department stepped back from the bond market entirely. He credits Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent with capping long-end rates for now, but says that intervention only delays a reckoning, since neither party in Washington shows any willingness to cut spending. "We think Bitcoin can effectively go to infinity versus the dollar." — Matt Cole, on Bloomberg https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NFQVh9AH0lM That logic underpins Strive's public forecast of a 50% compound annual growth rate for Bitcoin through 2030, a figure Cole calls conservative given the asset's past bull-market cycles, a view he first laid out when he called the bear market over last month. It also explains why Strive's SATA preferred stock, which pays a daily cash dividend, has, according to Cole, outperformed Bitcoin itself by more than 100% in 2026 even as BTC has traded roughly flat. Why the Treasury Model Persists Cole also pushed back on the idea that the Bitcoin treasury company model is fading. He argues it never broke, only that firms without a clear thesis or sound debt terms struggled once the bear market hit, while disciplined buyers kept accumulating even as Wall Street treasuries resumed buying. Cole's framing puts Bitcoin's price action second to a wager on US fiscal dysfunction, one that only pays off if bond markets and the dollar move the way he expects over the next several years. articles.title: Vista Gold (VGZ) Agrees to Sale. Can its Buyer Fund the Mt Todd Gold Mine?
articles.content: Vista Gold (VGZ) Agrees to Sale. Can its Buyer Fund the Mt Todd Gold Mine? Jeff Lewis September 22, 2026 3 min read VGZ Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN: VGZ ) announced on September 21 that it had agreed to be acquired by Artemis Gold Inc. (TSXV:ARTG). Under the agreement signed September 20, shareholders would receive 0.0966 buyer common shares for each existing common share and own approximately 5% of the combined company. That ownership calculation excludes the buyer's existing 4.95% stake in Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN:VGZ), which it intends to cancel at completion. For shareholders, the trade-off is a smaller interest in a larger mining business with an operating asset and development expertise. The central question is whether that combination can supply the capital and execution needed to bring Australia's Mt Todd gold project into production. Why Vista Gold Corp (VGZ) Mining Stock Is Skyrocketing So Far In 2025? Bull Case Artemis Gold Inc. (TSXV:ARTG) operates the Blackwater mine in British Columbia and expects its future cash generation to support Mt Todd. That offers Vista Gold a potential funding source alongside a team experienced in building and operating mines. The financial starting point explains the appeal. Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN:VGZ) ended June 2026 with $49.5 million in cash and no debt. Management described that cash as sufficient for interim development objectives. Joining an operating producer could broaden the resources available for the much larger task of construction. The acquisition requires no cash consideration or new acquisition debt. Preserving the buyer's financial capacity could leave more room for investment, although the share exchange itself does not raise construction funding. Shareholders would also gain exposure to operating cash flows while waiting for Mt Todd. If Blackwater's expansions perform as planned, the combined business could fund development with less dependence on a separate project-financing package. That could improve the prospects of turning a development asset into an operating mine. Bear Case Mt Todd would sit behind other projects in the spending queue. Blackwater's Phase 1A and EP2 expansions remain the priority, with EP2 completion expected by mid-2028. Mt Todd construction spending is expected after EP2 reaches full production. That sequence makes funding dependent on execution elsewhere. Expansion delays, higher costs, or weaker gold prices could reduce the cash available for Mt Todd. Investors need to distinguish expected future cash generation from money committed to a construction budget. The ownership trade-off also matters. Holders of Vista Gold Corp. (NYSEAMERICAN:VGZ) would exchange their standalone investment for a minority interest in the combined business. Their returns would increasingly depend on the buyer's broader capital-allocation decisions, including how much cash goes to Blackwater, Mt Todd or shareholder distributions. Story Continues Closing is targeted for January 2027, subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals. Until those conditions are satisfied, the proposed development route remains contingent on completing the acquisition. A construction budget, financing schedule, and successful Blackwater expansion would provide stronger evidence that access to a producing partner can translate into a funded mine. (NASDAQ: MTSI ) announced a 3.2-terabit optical chipset on September 17 built around eight 448-Gbps PAM-4 channels. A day later, BMO Capital upgraded the shares to Outperform with a $335 target, arguing that a 36% decline from the May peak had compressed MACOM's forward valuation to roughly 29 times earnings while data-center fundamentals remained intact. That puts Coherent Corp. (NYSE: COHR ) directly in the conversation because both companies supply the optical connectivity needed to keep larger AI clusters fed with data. Faster GPUs Need Faster Networks MACOM's new platform combines drivers, photodiodes and transimpedance amplifiers for next-generation optical modules. As links move toward 3.2T, higher-speed optical modules require more sophisticated analog and photonic components. A single supplier that can provide both transmit and receive building blocks can also reduce customer qualification work. The catch is price. Even after the pullback BMO highlighted, MACOM has already been rerated around AI networking. Continued upside requires the new products to convert technical leadership into revenue faster than rivals. Coherent Corp. (NYSE:COHR) brings much greater scale in data-center optics and has become one of the market's better-known beneficiaries of AI networking demand. Scale can help Coherent capture broad volume as 800G, 1.6T and eventually faster links proliferate. It also makes the company more exposed if hyperscaler deployments or optical pricing soften. Hedge funds moved in opposite directions Insider Monkey's Q2 data showed MACOM ownership rising to 59 hedge funds from 45 in Q1. AI clusters require so much bandwidth that several suppliers can grow simultaneously. What MACOM's new chipset changes is the comparison. A stock that spent years outside the center of the AI trade is now shipping components aimed directly at the next generation of links, and Wall Street has started paying attention. articles.title: May Mobility's SPAC Merger: Is This a Road to Nowhere for Investors?
articles.content: May Mobility's SPAC Merger: Is This a Road to Nowhere for Investors? Daniel Miller, The Motley Fool September 22, 2026 6 min read ACGC NVDA Investors eager to buy into the futuristic vision of profitable driverless vehicles will get their chance soon . May Mobility is aiming to become the first U.S. publicly listed pure-play option for an autonomous ride-hailing technology company. It is poised to go public through a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), merging with ACP Holdings Acquisition (NASDAQ: ACGC) that values the combined company at roughly $1.4 billion. It's expected to operate as May Mobility. trading on the Nasdaq exchange under MAY. But before investors get too excited, let's pump the brakes and take a look at the details. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Opportunity knocks It's easy for investors to get excited about the opportunity, but many might not be aware of the potential market size or growth prospects. The global robotaxi market is projected to reach about $415 billion by 2035, with the U.S. accounting for a roughly $48 billion slice of that pie. The fleet of U.S. commercial autonomous vehicles (AVs) is projected to expand from only about 4,000 vehicles currently to around 35,000 by 2030 -- or about 8% of the ride-sharing market. A year ago this month, Bank of America projected that the long-term U.S. total addressable market (TAM) for AV ride-hailing is a trillion-dollar opportunity as companies such as May Mobility aim to replace the drivers that take roughly 70% of every fare. It's also important for investors to realize how early in the game this is: Alphabet 's Waymo, with an estimated $350 million in annualized revenue, would represent only about 0.5% of U.S. ride-hailing bookings. The opportunity is potentially lucrative, albeit still very early in the game. So, what makes May Mobility intriguing? An asset-light transition May Mobility is moving to an asset-light model. At the company's initial U.S. ride-hailing launch site, it estimates the costs for the safety driver; vehicles (financing, depreciation, insurance, maintenance); site operations (fuel/charging, depot operations, and staff); and remote vehicle supervisors, software maintenance, and field engineers. In this asset-heavy scenario, May Mobility's projections put its annual revenue per vehicle between $130,000 to $150,000, as it keeps all the revenue. But because it also incurs all the costs, it checks in with a negative gross margin per vehicle with a safety driver. Story Continues Under its asset-light model, which includes removing the safety driver, May Mobility transfers the vehicle costs as well as the site operating costs to a fleet operating partner, although it will still incur the costs for remote supervisors, field engineers, and software maintenance. This scenario would come with a larger fleet size thanks to a fleet-operator partner, and lower revenue ($50,000 to $72,000 per vehicle) as it splits the sales with that partner. But it checks in with a gross margin per vehicle between $35,000 to $50,000 annually because it would push off significant costs and could scale up more quickly without needing to purchase and own the fleet. There's further upside with management targeting a 50% reduction in its bill of materials (BOM) by the end of 2028. That's from cost savings realized through computing and sensors with next-generation chip alternatives and as lidar/radar/camera markets scale up and mature. May Mobility also expects to reduce its BOM through cost reductions in hardware components and integration when its software could be installed by the original equipment manufacturer (with Toyota as a partner for AV-ready vehicle platforms at scale) rather than installing it in vehicles afterwards. Over the long term without drivers, management is targeting gross margins of about 70%, and margins under earnings before interest and taxes around 30%. How going public helps When the SPAC deal and merger closes, it could provide May Mobility with up to $337 million in funding. Investors can look at the economics and do the math: In 2025, the company generated roughly $10 million in revenue with a 27% gross margin, while burning $93 million in cash. The SPAC funds should enable it to strengthen its balance sheet and liquidity, finance added research and development, invest in the supply chain to reduce costs, and launch new in markets without drivers. However, without a major cash pile, the cash burn could erode its liquidity rather quickly. What it all means It's an exciting time in an automotive industry that's poised to evolve rapidly over the next decade. However, investors must understand that this is an exceptionally high-risk investment currently. May Mobility's 27% gross margin is an encouraging beginning, but the cash burn is significant and will only increase in the near term. It will rely heavily on the $337 million of fresh capital from its public debut, and that could erode rapidly. Investors also have to consider that despite being in the early innings, there are some heavyweights accelerating forward, including market leader Waymo and Tesla 's slow but steady progress with its Cybercab business. Tesla's Cybercab. Image source: Tesla. May Mobility is intriguing, but this only scratches the surface. Potential shareholders must read through the investor presentation, available here , and recognize that this could end in a total loss. For now, this should be a company that most retail investors watch curiously from the sidelines, especially as this debut tests investor demand for a pure-play AV ride-hailing company. Should you buy stock in ACP Holdings Acquisition Corp. right now? articles.title: SK Hynix Is Eyeing Intel’s (INTC) Ohio Site. Why Micron (MU) Should Pay Attention
articles.content: SK Hynix Is Eyeing Intel’s (INTC) Ohio Site. Why Micron (MU) Should Pay Attention Habib Ur Rehman September 22, 2026 3 min read INTC SKHY MU SK Hynix is exploring something it has never done before: manufacturing memory chips in the United States. Reuters reported on September 16 that the Korean memory giant is discussing several possibilities with Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC ), including leasing part of Intel's long-delayed Ohio complex or forming a venture involving Intel and large cloud customers. SK Hynix said no specific plan has been finalized. For Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU ), the talks matter because one of its strongest strategic advantages is being the major U.S.-based memory producer while AI has made DRAM and HBM increasingly scarce. SK Hynix May Move Into Intel’s $100 Billion Ohio Fab. Micron Has a Reason to Watch SK Hynix Could Give Intel Another Path for Its Delayed Ohio Site Intel has committed enormous capital to Ohio, with the broader project potentially reaching around $100 billion over time. Delays have pushed planned production into the next decade. A tenant or joint-venture partner could therefore help Intel share the financial burden of developing the Ohio site rather than relying entirely on its own foundry demand to justify the buildout. That is the bull case. The bear case is that exploratory talks are a long way from revenue. Bringing advanced Korean memory production to the U.S. could face cost problems, technology-transfer restrictions and objections from Seoul. Intel still needs its core manufacturing roadmap to work. Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) sits on the other side of the equation. AI demand has pushed memory pricing and availability into a strong cycle, and Micron is already pursuing a large U.S. manufacturing expansion. More domestic manufacturing incentives and customer interest in secure supply support that plan. A successful SK Hynix move could eventually erode part of Micron's U.S.-supply differentiation. U.S. cloud companies would gain another potential domestic supplier, while additional long-term memory capacity could eventually loosen the market that currently supports exceptional pricing. Hedge funds loaded up on both chipmakers Insider Monkey tracked 138 hedge funds holding Intel in Q2, up sharply from 112 in Q1. AQR Capital Management held roughly 10.7 million shares after trimming its stake about 7%. Micron's count rose to 184 funds from 154, one of the stronger quarter-over-quarter increases among large semiconductor names. Coatue Management expanded its MU stake dramatically during the quarter. Intel had about 152.2 million shares sold short as of August 31, roughly 3% of public float and 1.7 days to cover. The talks do not rescue Intel's foundry strategy or weaken Micron overnight. They do show what AI scarcity is doing to the supply chain. Memory manufacturing is becoming strategic enough that SK Hynix is considering putting advanced capacity on American soil, and Intel's delayed Ohio project suddenly gives it a potentially valuable asset to negotiate with. articles.title: Pat Gelsinger Just Backed a $100 Million Challenge to Nvidia’s AI Networking Moat. AMD Could Benefit
articles.content: Pat Gelsinger Just Backed a $100 Million Challenge to Nvidia’s AI Networking Moat. AMD Could Benefit Habib Ur Rehman September 22, 2026 3 min read NVDA AMD INTC Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger is backing a startup that thinks AI's next bottleneck is not the accelerator. It is everything waiting for data to arrive. Delos Data announced on September 15 that it raised more than $100 million to develop networking chips and software for increasingly heterogeneous AI data centers. Playground Global, where Gelsinger is a general partner, joined the round. Reuters reported that Delos is designing the network to work across different types of compute hardware rather than assuming every accelerator comes from NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ). That makes Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD ) an important read-through even though AMD is not an investor in Delos. Pat Gelsinger Just Backed a $100 Million Attack on Nvidia’s AI Networking Moat. AMD Could Benefit For illustration purposes only. Photo by Brett Sayles on Pexels Open networking attacks the strongest part of Nvidia's stack Nvidia does not dominate AI simply because its GPUs are fast. NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) sells a tightly integrated system of accelerators, networking, interconnects and software. That makes large clusters easier to deploy and gives customers fewer reasons to mix architectures. Delos is betting the market becomes less uniform as inference expands. Its pitch is that a data center should be able to connect whatever mix of accelerators makes economic sense. Gelsinger described idle compute waiting for data as a major waste of both money and energy. If that architecture works, AMD benefits indirectly. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) has been improving Instinct accelerator performance and winning AI deployments, but every friction point involved in mixing AMD hardware with another vendor's ecosystem protects Nvidia. Hardware-agnostic networking could lower that friction. The counterargument is brutal: Nvidia already has scale, mature software and networking products customers know work. A startup with $100 million of financing is attacking an incumbent that spends billions on research and sells the full rack. Delos also has to prove its claimed performance improvements in commercial deployments. Hedge funds increased exposure to both incumbents Insider Monkey tracked 285 hedge funds holding Nvidia in Q2, up from 275 in Q1. Arrowstreet Capital raised its position 10% to roughly 34.7 million shares. AMD's holder count climbed to 164 from 134, while Marshall Wace held approximately 3.9 million shares after increasing its stake modestly. AMD had about 41.7 million shares sold short as of August 31, equal to roughly 2.6% of float and 2.5 days to cover. Story Continues Delos does not have to replace Nvidia networking to matter. It only has to make mixed AI clusters easier to build. Nvidia's moat is strongest when customers buy the entire system together. Anything that makes the pieces more interchangeable gives AMD and every other accelerator challenger a slightly wider door. articles.title: Lumentum Jumped Nearly 10% While Corning Barely Moved. Is the AI Optics Trade Splitting Apart?
articles.content: Lumentum Jumped Nearly 10% While Corning Barely Moved. Is the AI Optics Trade Splitting Apart? Habib Ur Rehman September 22, 2026 3 min read LITE GLW COHR ^GSPC When AI stocks rebounded last week, optical networking companies did not rebound equally. Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: LITE ) jumped nearly 10% in Wednesday trading and led the S&P 500, while Coherent rose 6.9%. Corning Incorporated (NYSE: GLW ) managed only a 0.4% gain and remained down sharply for the week. All three sit inside the same broad AI-connectivity buildout. The divergence suggests investors are beginning to distinguish between different pieces of that infrastructure rather than buying every optics name together. Lumentum Jumped Nearly 10% While Corning Barely Moved. The AI Optics Trade Is Splitting Apart Photo from Lumentum Holdings website Lumentum offers concentrated exposure to the bandwidth problem AI clusters increasingly need optical connections as more accelerators communicate across larger physical distances. That drives demand for high-speed transceivers, lasers and other photonic components. For Lumentum Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:LITE), concentrated exposure is both the attraction and the risk. Strong hyperscaler spending can create powerful operating leverage as faster generations of optical links ramp. The same concentration can produce violent corrections when investors question the pace of AI spending or customer deployments. Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW) has a broader business and participates through optical fiber and connectivity infrastructure. The company benefits as hyperscalers build new campuses and connect larger networks, but that exposure is less directly tied to the highest-value transceiver components. Corning also introduced a fresh complication. A September filing established an equity distribution agreement allowing the company to sell up to $2 billion of stock through Goldman Sachs. That gives Corning capital flexibility for large projects, but potential issuance creates dilution at a moment when investors are already scrutinizing the cost of AI infrastructure expansion. Professional investors also split on the two names Insider Monkey's database showed Lumentum ownership falling to 111 hedge funds in Q2 from 123 in Q1. Arrowstreet Capital nevertheless increased its position sharply during the quarter. Corning moved the other way, rising to 99 hedge-fund holders from 91, while Tairen Capital increased its GLW position by roughly 9%. Lumentum's August 31 short interest stood at about 7.12 million shares, nearly 8% of public float, with approximately 1.7 days to cover. That makes positioning meaningfully heavier than in many large-cap AI infrastructure names. The takeaway from the rebound is not that Lumentum won and Corning lost. Their economics are different. Lumentum offers more concentrated exposure to high-speed optical components, while Corning offers broader exposure to the fiber-heavy physical buildout underneath them. When the AI trade becomes selective, that distinction suddenly matters. articles.content: Intel (INTC) Could Get a Fresh Valuation for Altera. AMD (AMD) Is the Rival to Watch Habib Ur Rehman September 22, 2026 3 min read INTC AMD Intel sold control of Altera last year. Now the programmable-chip company is heading back toward the public market just as AI gives investors a new reason to care about FPGAs. Altera said on September 15 that it confidentially filed for a U.S. IPO. Reuters previously reported that the offering could raise more than $2 billion. Silver Lake owns 51% after investing $4.46 billion for control, while Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC ) retains 49%. Intel’s Former FPGA Business Filed for a $2 Billion-Plus IPO. AMD Is the Rival to Watch Intel Corp.'s headquarters, the Robert Noyce Building in Santa Clara, California. Photo from Intel Corp website The most useful strategic comparison is Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMD ), which bought FPGA leader Xilinx in 2022 and integrated programmable silicon into a much broader data-center portfolio. The IPO could put a price on an asset Intel partially kept Intel bought Altera for $16.7 billion in 2015 before separating the business and selling control to Silver Lake. An IPO would create a new market valuation for Intel Corporation's (NASDAQ:INTC) remaining interest. That matters because Intel needs capital. Its foundry expansion requires enormous spending while the company is still trying to restore competitiveness in conventional CPUs and advanced manufacturing. A strong Altera valuation could therefore crystallize value in an asset investors currently bury inside Intel's much larger turnaround. The downside is that IPO appetite for anything carrying an AI label can run ahead of operating reality. Altera makes programmable chips across industrial, communications, aerospace and data-center markets. Management has projected mid-20% revenue growth in 2026, but investors will still have to determine how much of that growth is genuinely AI-driven. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) shows what Altera ultimately has to compete against. Xilinx gave AMD FPGAs, adaptive SoCs and software that can sit beside its EPYC CPUs and Instinct accelerators. That bundle can be attractive in heterogeneous systems. The bear case is that AMD paid heavily to assemble that portfolio, and integrating multiple product families does not guarantee every FPGA workload migrates into AMD's ecosystem. Funds became much more interested in both chipmakers Insider Monkey counted 138 hedge funds holding Intel in Q2, up from 112 in Q1. AQR Capital Management held about 10.7 million shares after trimming its stake roughly 7%. AMD ownership jumped to 164 funds from 134, while Marshall Wace held about 3.9 million shares after a modest increase. Intel had approximately 152.2 million shares sold short on August 31, about 3% of public float. Story Continues Altera's offering terms have not been set, so $2 billion remains a reported fundraising possibility rather than a finalized deal. What the IPO could do is make a hidden part of Intel easier to value while giving investors a fresh public benchmark against AMD's Xilinx strategy. articles.content: Why Bernstein Still Sees 46% Upside in Zscaler (ZS) but Downgraded Palo Alto (PANW) Habib Ur Rehman September 22, 2026 3 min read ZS PANW Wall Street has spent much of 2026 rewarding cybersecurity stocks for the risks created by AI. Bernstein now thinks the easy part of that trade is over, with one major exception. Bernstein analyst Peter Weed raised his target on Zscaler, Inc. articles.title: “The New Clippy”: Benioff Uses Salesforce’s Biggest Product Launch in Years to Challenge Microsoft
articles.content: “The New Clippy”: Benioff Uses Salesforce’s Biggest Product Launch in Years to Challenge Microsoft Sheryar Siddiq September 22, 2026 4 min read CRM MSFT Marc Benioff is never one to pass up a chance to take a jab at Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT ), and Dreamforce 2026 was no different. The Salesforce CEO used the company's flagship annual conference in San Francisco to announce AIforce, the biggest product launch Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE: CRM ) has made in years, and to once again refer to Microsoft's Copilot as "the new Clippy," doubling down on a dig he made two years ago. What is Salesforce's (CRM) Economic Moat, and is it Widening or Narrowing? What AIforce Actually Does Salesforce is positioning AIforce as an open, provider-agnostic layer rather than a single proprietary assistant. It's intended to work across multiple AI systems, including Anthropic's Claude, via a specific integration called Claudeforce, which Salesforce claims guarantees zero data retention by the model provider, as well as ChatGPT, Slack, and other environments. Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) made the announcement alongside an additional strategic marker: a fiscal 2030 revenue target of $63 billion, which management reiterated at Dreamforce. A Rivalry That Goes Back To 2024 Benioff portrayed AIforce as the solution to what he calls the "Fantasyland" problem, arguing that competing AI solutions, including Copilot, lack the dependable, controlled business-data layer required to consistently run enterprise operations. It's a continuation of a public feud that's been going on since at least Dreamforce 2024, when Benioff first compared Copilot to Clippy, Microsoft's widely mocked, uninvited desktop assistant from the late 1990s, saying, "We all know now that Microsoft Copilot is basically the new Microsoft Clippy, that customers have not gotten value from it." He's returned to that theme several times since, including at Davos, in an October 2024 written critique saying that Microsoft "lacks the data, metadata, and enterprise security models to create real corporate intelligence," and on a podcast where he labeled Copilot a "tremendous disservice" to the AI sector. Favorable Analyst Response Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) shares closed at $255.65 on September 15, after a nearly 34% rally in the previous month following a rough start to 2026 that saw the stock tumble as much as 37%. That momentum was fueled by Salesforce's most recent quarterly results, which featured $11.35 billion in revenue, exceeding Wall Street's projections on both the top and bottom lines. Analyst reaction to the Dreamforce announcements was also favorable, with Stifel raising its price target for Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) to $300 from $275 while reaffirming a Buy rating, citing six distinct revenue channels laid out by the company for monetizing its new AI stack, including additional core licenses, premium SKU upgrades, Agentforce spending, Data 360, Agent Fabric and Guardian, and APIs, MCPs and related infrastructure. Story Continues Institutional Positioning Institutional posture shifted in similar directions for the two competitors. Salesforce, Inc. (NYSE:CRM) saw hedge fund ownership fall slightly, from 101 in the first quarter to 99 in the second. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) experienced a greater fall, from 282 funds to 273, though both declines predate the Dreamforce event and are more likely to reflect broader software-sector positioning moves than a direct read on this contest. How AIforce Takes On Copilot Salesforce's pitch for AIforce as an open layer that brings Salesforce data, permissions and business logic into Claude, ChatGPT and other AI interfaces could still be an important competitive distinction, particularly for companies that want to use Salesforce context across multiple AI environments. The emphasis on regulated data access and zero data retention in Claudeforce directly addresses enterprise trust problems, which have hampered AI adoption elsewhere. Conference Hype, Unclear Pricing, and Microsoft's Distribution Juggernaut However, Salesforce's stock has a documented history of rallying on analyst upgrades and conference announcements before reversing those gains, as seen with earlier JPMorgan and Citi buy calls in 2026, and pricing and adoption uncertainty around Agentforce remain unanswered questions even as new products pile on top of it. Microsoft's competition is also far from theoretical, considering Copilot's distribution advantage via Office and Dynamics 365. Insider Monkey's Bottom Line Investors should keep an eye on whether this round of enthusiasm lasts longer than previous Dreamforce-fueled surges, with confirmation likely to come from the next quarterly report, which will show whether Agentforce and now AIforce adoption numbers are translating into the kind of Data and AI revenue growth analysts are projecting with their newly set $300 price targets. Given the remaining uncertainty around how quickly Salesforce can convert AI adoption into meaningful revenue, the more reliable signal for investors will be concrete adoption and revenue-conversion data in upcoming earnings, rather than the announcement itself or the pre-Dreamforce rally that followed Salesforce's latest earnings report. While we acknowledge the potential of CRM as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. articles.title: Nike (NKE): Wall Street Tests Whether the Turnaround Can Outrun Weak Demand Ahead of Q1 Results
articles.content: Nike (NKE): Wall Street Tests Whether the Turnaround Can Outrun Weak Demand Ahead of Q1 Results Faheem Tahir September 22, 2026 5 min read NKE NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) heads into its October 1 fiscal 2027 first-quarter report with Wall Street focused less on whether revenue can beat a modest guide and more on whether improving margins and performance categories can offset weak demand in the lifestyle business. The latest warning comes from Stifel, which cut its price target to $40 from $45 on September 21 while keeping a Hold rating. The firm expects a more promotional Western marketplace and a tougher fiscal fourth-quarter gross-margin comparison, cutting its FY2027 and FY2028 adjusted EPS estimates by $0.20 each, to $1.70 and $2.05. Nike (NKE): Wall Street Tests Whether the Turnaround Can Outrun Weak Demand Ahead of Q1 Results Mbuso Sydwell Nkosi/Shutterstock.com The Bull Case: Sport, Wholesale and the World Cup Can Buy Nike Time There are still tangible signs that NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE)'s reset is working in parts of the portfolio. Performance grew mid-single digits in fiscal 2026, while Running posted five consecutive quarters of double-digit growth and added roughly $1 billion in revenue. North American wholesale revenue grew 10% in the fourth quarter, and management said the business benefited from lower returns, cancellations and discounts rather than simply pushing more inventory into stores. The World Cup provides another near-term tailwind. Stifel estimates the tournament could add about $300 million to Q1 revenue, while NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) has already pointed to stronger football demand and said its World Cup product launches were gaining traction. Stifel also continues to expect revenue above consensus, noting that Nike has exceeded its own revenue guidance for seven consecutive quarters. Margin improvement could provide another offset. NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE)'s Q4 gross margin, excluding the $986 million tariff-recovery benefit, was down just 10 basis points year-over-year, better than its guidance. Management attributed the improvement partly to lower discounts, cancellations and sales-related reserves and expects supply-chain restructuring to support margins in FY2027. The Bear Case: The New Product Pipeline Still Has to Prove Itself The problem is that NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE)'s strongest performance categories are not yet large enough to erase weakness elsewhere. Sportswear declined double digits in Q4, while management expects Sportswear and Jordan streetwear to remain negative through FY2027, even with improvement in the second half. Together, those businesses represent roughly half of revenue. That is where Stifel's latest update becomes important. The firm sees insufficient consumer demand for Nike's new products and continued contraction in Hoops Classics, which represents about 18% of revenue. UBS has also pointed to deteriorating global sales trends and expects a Q1 EPS miss, while Citi sees elevated promotions and difficult North American comparisons weighing on Q2. Baird similarly cited weaker marketplace conditions, more negative retailer commentary on athletic lifestyle sales and pressure from Nike's China e-commerce reset. Story Continues China remains another unresolved drag. Greater China revenue fell 17% in Q4, and management expects near-term trends to remain broadly consistent with that decline. Although full-price realization and sell-through have improved in some areas, NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) is still cleaning up inventory and reducing supply into the market. Valuation Premium Faces Growing Skepticism Nike's valuation and positioning add another layer to that debate. The stock traded at a 20.66 forward P/E as of September 21, compared with 10.46 for Deckers Outdoor, 14.27 for On Holding and 11.47 for Adidas. Hedge fund ownership also fell to 56 funds in the second quarter from 71 in the first, although several individual managers increased their stakes sharply. Arrowstreet Capital raised its position 10,175% to 5.62 million shares, while Renaissance Technologies increased its stake 1,192% to 4.07 million shares. Meanwhile, short interest climbed to 75.59 million shares as of August 31 from 57.37 million a month earlier, putting short interest at 7.92% of the float and 5.10% of shares outstanding. The combination leaves NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) with a higher valuation than several peers alongside reduced hedge fund participation and rising short interest, making evidence of a broader recovery increasingly important. The Takeaway: Q1 Is About the Quality of the Recovery The October 1 report therefore faces a higher bar than the headline revenue number suggests. A World Cup boost can support sales, but Wall Street is looking for evidence that demand is broadening beyond Running and football, particularly in Sportswear and Jordan, while gross-margin improvement survives a more promotional marketplace. That tension explains the recent estimate cuts despite some analysts retaining relatively constructive revenue expectations. UBS expects a Q1 EPS shortfall (five cents) and sees risk of a broader FY2027 reset at the November Investor Day, while BMO expects NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE) to reset its FY2027 outlook when it reports. For NIKE, Inc. (NYSE:NKE), the key question heading into October 1 is whether the turnaround is beginning to create healthier full-price demand, or merely shifting the mix toward the parts of the portfolio that are already working. The answer will also shape expectations heading into the November 16-17 Investor Day, where management is scheduled to outline the next phase of its growth strategy. While we acknowledge the potential of NKE as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk.
